summary:
I've spent time this cycle on the machinery behind Hermes-Agent, my personal automation assistant, rather than user-facing features. A version bump silently renamed every MCP tool from single to double underscores, and the error message you got back when you called the old name — "not a deferrable tool" — read like a permissions problem when it actually just meant the tool didn't exist anymore. The model didn't know that, so it retried, wrapped calls in workarounds, and wrote itself memory notes about how to fix a problem that wasn't there. Fixing it meant sweeping every skill file and stored memory for the old names and checking each one against what the server actually exposes now, not guessing from the old convention.

On BudgetTracker I built out the read-only tool surface the agent uses to answer questions about spending — burn rate, upcoming obligations, cash flow projections. The rule I kept coming back to: any number the agent shows has to come from a SQL query, never from the model doing arithmetic on numbers in its context. That sounds obvious until you're debugging why a "you're over budget" alert fired for an account with no budget set — the fix was excluding that case at the query level, not trusting the model to notice the denominator was zero.

Switchboard is a small proxy that sits in front of a single shared GPU and arbitrates between everything that wants to use it — the chat model, image generation, a couple of side experiments. Recently I stood up a second model behind it just to A/B against the one already in production, on the theory that a newer architecture might be better at picking the right tool mid-conversation. Both scored identically on my test harness, which told me less about the models than about the harness — it was testing with a handful of clean mock tools, and the actual failures happen with thirty-plus real tool schemas and near-duplicate names. Negative result, but a more honest one than the number would've suggested on its own.

Most of what I ship day to day is unglamorous plumbing like this: get the retry logic right, get the error messages to actually say what's wrong, make sure a benchmark is testing the thing you think it's testing. It adds up slower than a new feature, but it's the difference between an agent you can leave running unattended and one you have to babysit.

highlights.oneLiner: swept tool names after an upgrade silently renamed every MCP tool
built read-only spending/forecast tools, math kept in SQL not the model
A/B'd a second model behind the GPU proxy against the production one
